questions.stem: Amaka has ₦2,000 and must choose between a novel and a pair of sandals, each costing ₦2,000. She buys the sandals. Her opportunity cost is
options: the ₦2,000 she spent on the sandals
the profit made by the shoe seller
the interest she could earn on ₦2,000 in a bank
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone, which here is the novel.

questions.stem: A list of a person's unsatisfied wants arranged in order of importance is called
questions.explanation: The scale of preference ranks wants in order of urgency so that the most pressing are satisfied first.

questions.stem: A point lying outside a country's production possibility curve represents a combination of goods that
options: is produced when the country is in a recession
cannot be produced with the resources and technology now available
will be produced if workers are paid higher wages
can be produced only when some resources are left idle
shows the most efficient use of the existing resources
questions.explanation: Points beyond the frontier are unattainable with present resources and technology.

questions.stem: An outward shift of the whole production possibility curve of Nigeria would most likely be caused by
options: an increase in unemployment in the economy
a reduction in the number of workers in the country
a movement of resources from farming into manufacturing
a fall in the price of imported consumer goods
new mineral discoveries and improved technology
questions.explanation: More resources or better technology raise the maximum output of both goods, shifting the whole curve outward.

questions.stem: A fisherman in Bayelsa who catches fish for sale is engaged in
questions.explanation: Extraction of natural resources such as fishing, mining and farming is primary production.

questions.stem: Of the following occupations found in Anambra State, the one classified as a tertiary activity is
options: Running a bus service between Enugu and Onitsha
Weaving aso-oke cloth by hand in an Iseyin textile workshop
questions.explanation: Tertiary activities provide services; transport is a service, while the others are primary or secondary activities.

questions.stem: A production possibility curve that is concave (bowed outward) to the origin shows that
options: the economy can produce unlimited quantities of both goods
output of both goods can rise without reallocating resources
resources are equally suited to the production of both goods
the opportunity cost of each good remains constant throughout
the opportunity cost of a good rises as more of it is produced
questions.explanation: Because resources are not equally suited to all uses, more and more of one good must be given up for each extra unit of the other.

questions.stem: Economics is best described as a social science because it
options: studies how plants and animals interact with nature
relies only on controlled laboratory experiments
studies human behaviour in using scarce resources
deals mainly with the printing and use of money
is concerned with the physical properties of goods
questions.explanation: Economics studies how people, as members of society, choose between alternative uses of scarce resources.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur who organises the other factors and bears the risks of a business is rewarded with
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur bears risk and receives profit; rent goes to land, wages to labour and interest to capital.

questions.stem: A feature that distinguishes land from the other factors of production is that
options: it can be increased at will by government
questions.explanation: Land is a free gift of nature, fixed in total supply and geographically immobile.

questions.stem: A tractor bought by a farmer in Benue State is an example of
questions.explanation: Capital consists of man-made goods used to produce other goods.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is performed only by the entrepreneur?
options: Bearing the uninsurable risks of the business
Lending money to the firm at a fixed rate of interest
Supplying physical effort on the production line
Providing natural resources used in production
Maintaining and repairing machines in the factory
questions.explanation: Uninsurable risk-bearing and final decision-making are the special functions of the entrepreneur.

questions.stem: The efficiency of labour can be improved mainly through
options: an increase in the size of the total population
the use of more land in the production process
a general reduction in the wage rate paid
training, good health and better working conditions
longer working hours without any rest periods
questions.explanation: Education, training, health and conditions of work raise the productivity of each worker.

questions.stem: Depreciation of capital refers to
options: a fall in the rate of interest paid on borrowed funds
loss in value of capital goods through wear and obsolescence
the money set aside to pay workers' monthly salaries
the conversion of household savings into investment
the increase in the stock of capital goods over time
questions.explanation: Capital goods wear out or become outdated; this loss of value is depreciation or capital consumption.

questions.stem: Capital formation in an economy depends most directly on
options: the size of the labour force on its own
the volume of imported consumer goods
the number of public holidays declared in a year
the quantity of land available for farming
the level of savings and their productive investment
questions.explanation: Capital formation is the creation of new capital goods, which requires savings to be channelled into investment.

questions.stem: Labour as a factor of production refers to
options: the land on which a factory is built
money borrowed to start a new business
all natural resources found on the earth
human effort, mental or physical, used in production
machines and tools used in factories
questions.explanation: Labour is human effort, both physical and mental, applied to production; its reward is wages.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: In a capitalist economic system, the means of production are mainly owned by
options: the state on behalf of the people
questions.explanation: Private ownership of resources and the profit motive are the main features of capitalism.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Under a socialist economic system, the basic economic questions are answered mainly by
questions.explanation: In a planned economy a central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Economists classify the Nigerian economy as mixed mainly because
options: there is no private ownership of land in the country
foreign firms are not allowed to operate in the country
both government and private persons own means of production
all businesses in the country are owned by government
prices of all goods are fixed by the government
questions.explanation: In a mixed economy the public and private sectors coexist, each owning and controlling some resources.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: A major disadvantage of the capitalist system is that
options: income and wealth may be unequally distributed
new products are rarely developed by firms
consumers have no freedom of choice at all in the market
there is no incentive for hard work or saving
production is decided by the government only
questions.explanation: Private ownership and profit-seeking can concentrate income and wealth in a few hands.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Consumer sovereignty is a feature of
questions.explanation: Under capitalism consumers' spending decisions guide what producers make.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of a centrally planned economy?
options: Prices adjust quickly to changes in demand and supply
Individuals are free to start any business they like
Resources can be directed to national priorities
The profit motive encourages efficiency in all firms
Producers compete freely to attract consumers
questions.explanation: Central planning allows the state to channel resources to chosen priorities, though often at the cost of efficiency and choice.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: The "for whom to produce" question in an economy is concerned with
options: how output is shared among members of society
the best location for new industries
the quantity of goods to be imported each year
the choice of production techniques to be used
the types and quantities of goods to be produced
questions.explanation: "For whom" deals with the distribution of output, which depends on how income is shared.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: The price mechanism allocates resources in
questions.explanation: In a free market economy the forces of demand and supply, expressed through prices, allocate resources.

questions.stem: The ages of six SS3 students are 16, 17, 16, 18, 16 and 19 years. The mode is
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often; 16 occurs three times.

questions.stem: The daily sales (in ₦'000) of a provision shop over five days were 12, 15, 9, 20 and 14. The mean daily sale is
The median of the numbers 7, 3, 9, 12, 5 and 10 is
questions.explanation: Arranged: 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12; the median is the mean of the two middle values, (7 + 9)/2 = 8.

questions.stem: A pie chart shows how a family spends its monthly income of ₦240,000. If food takes ₦90,000, the angle of the sector for food is
A graph that uses bars of equal width whose heights show values is called
questions.explanation: A bar chart represents values by the heights (or lengths) of bars of equal width.

questions.stem: The mean of five numbers is 12. If four of them are 8, 10, 15 and 14, the fifth number is
Which of the following measures of central tendency is most affected by an extremely large value in a set of data?
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so one extreme value pulls it up; the median and mode are not much affected.

questions.stem:
In the frequency table below, x is the number of children per household in a village and f is the number of households.
x: 1, 2, 3, 4
f: 3, 5, 8, 4
The mean number of children per household is
According to the law of demand, when other factors are held constant,
options: the higher the price, the higher the quantity demanded
the quantity demanded is always equal to the quantity supplied
the higher the price, the lower the quantity demanded
price has no effect on the quantity demanded of a good
a rise in income reduces the demand for every good
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded vary inversely, ceteris paribus.

questions.stem: A rise in the price of petrol is most likely to reduce the demand for
questions.explanation: Cars and petrol are in joint demand (complements); a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other.

questions.stem: The demand for cement arising from the demand for new houses is an example of
questions.explanation: Cement is wanted not for itself but for the houses it helps to build, so its demand is derived.

questions.stem: Which of the following will cause the demand curve for rice, a normal good, to shift to the right?
options: An expected fall in the future price of rice
A fall in the price of rice
A rise in the price of rice
A fall in the price of beans, a substitute
questions.explanation: An increase in income raises demand at every price for a normal good, shifting the curve right; a change in its own price causes only a movement along the curve.

questions.stem: The price of a mathematical set rises from ₦1,500 to ₦1,800 and the number bought by a school bookshop falls from 600 to 480. Using the original price and quantity, the price elasticity of demand is
Mallam Sani buys less of a commodity each time his income rises, so his income elasticity of demand for it is negative. To him, the commodity is
questions.explanation: A negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, the mark of an inferior good.

questions.stem: One reason why a demand curve may slope upward from left to right is
options: a fall in consumers' money incomes
the buying of costly goods for prestige or show
the introduction of a sales tax on the good
a fall in the prices of close substitutes
an increase in the number of sellers in the market
questions.explanation: Goods bought for show (Veblen goods), Giffen goods and expectations of further price rises can give upward-sloping demand curves.

questions.stem: Demand for a commodity is said to be effective when
options: the government fixes its price by law
the consumer only wishes to own it
the commodity is given out free of charge
the commodity is produced in large quantities
the desire for it is backed by ability to pay
questions.explanation: Effective demand is desire supported by purchasing power at a given price.

questions.stem: The law of supply holds that, ceteris paribus,
options: more is supplied at lower prices than at higher prices
the quantity supplied does not change with price
supply is always equal to demand in every market
more is supplied at higher prices than at lower prices
sellers supply less whenever their costs fall
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable, so quantity supplied rises with price.

questions.stem: Beef and hides are an example of
questions.explanation: Producing beef automatically yields hides; the two are in joint (complementary) supply.

questions.stem: The supply curve of tomatoes reaching markets in Kano will shift to the left if there is
options: a government subsidy to tomato farmers
a rise in the price of tomatoes
a fall in the price of fertiliser
a pest attack on tomato farms
questions.explanation: A pest attack reduces the quantity offered at every price, shifting the supply curve to the left; a price change moves along the curve.

questions.stem: If a farmer can use the same land to grow either maize or cassava, maize and cassava are said to be in
questions.explanation: Resources used for one cannot be used for the other, so a rise in one's supply reduces the other's: competitive supply.

questions.stem: When the price of a good rises from ₦50 to ₦60, the quantity supplied rises from 200 to 260 units. Using the original values, the elasticity of supply is
The supply of fresh fish in a village market on a particular day is likely to be
questions.explanation: On the market day the quantity is fixed and must be sold before it spoils, so supply cannot respond to price.

questions.stem: A table showing the quantities of a commodity offered for sale at various prices is called
questions.explanation: A supply schedule lists quantities that sellers are willing to offer at different prices.

questions.stem: Elasticity of supply tends to be greater in the long run than in the short run because
options: producers have more time to adjust their inputs
all costs of production become fixed in the long run
consumers have more time to find substitutes
the government cannot change taxes in the short run
prices are held fixed by law in the long run
questions.explanation: Over time firms can expand capacity and new firms can enter, so output can respond more to price changes.

questions.stem: The satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming one additional unit of a commodity is called
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from consuming one more unit.

questions.stem: Tunde's total utility from eating successive oranges is 10, 18, 24, 28 and 30 utils. The marginal utility of the fourth orange is
questions.explanation: MU of the 4th orange = TU(4) − TU(3) = 28 − 24 = 4 utils.

questions.stem: Using Tunde's total utility figures of 10, 18, 24, 28 and 30 utils for one to five oranges, the average utility when three oranges are eaten is
questions.explanation: AU = TU/Q = 24/3 = 8 utils.

questions.stem: When total utility from a commodity is at its maximum, marginal utility is
options: equal to the price of the good
questions.explanation: Total utility rises while MU is positive and peaks where the next unit adds nothing, that is, MU = 0.

questions.stem: A consumer spends all her income on bread and eggs. The marginal utility of bread is 40 utils at a price of ₦400 and that of eggs is 30 utils at ₦200. To increase total satisfaction she should
options: buy more bread and fewer eggs
buy more eggs and less bread
buy equal quantities of both goods
questions.explanation: MU per naira is 0.1 for bread and 0.15 for eggs; shifting spending to eggs raises total utility until the ratios are equal.

questions.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium when
options: he buys equal quantities of all goods
marginal utility of every good is zero
he spends more on cheaper goods
total utility from each good is the same
the ratio of marginal utility to price is the same for all goods bought
questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb = … with all income spent.

questions.stem: Chidi enjoys his first bottle of chilled zobo far more than his third bottle on the same afternoon. This illustrates the principle that
options: consumer income falls as more is consumed
utility from each unit stays constant
marginal utility diminishes as consumption increases
total utility falls from the first unit onwards
the price of a good rises as more is bought
questions.explanation: Each successive unit gives less extra satisfaction than the one before it, after a point.

questions.stem: The downward slope of an individual's demand curve can be explained by the fact that
options: sellers prefer to sell large quantities
marginal utility falls as more units are consumed
price is fixed by the government
the consumer's income rises as price falls
questions.explanation: Since extra units give less satisfaction, a consumer buys more only at a lower price.

questions.stem: In a free market for sachet water, the market-clearing price is reached where
options: the government wants the water to be sold
sellers make the highest possible profit
buyers pay the lowest possible price
questions.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where the demand and supply curves intersect, so the market clears.

questions.stem: The demand and supply functions for a commodity are Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 20 + 3P. The equilibrium price is
Given Qd = 60 − 4P and Qs = −12 + 2P, the equilibrium quantity is
Suppose a state government orders that a bag of rice must not be sold above a ceiling that is lower than the market-clearing price. The likely outcome is
options: a surplus of the commodity in all the markets of the state
an increase in the quantity supplied
a shortage of the commodity and black marketing
a fall in demand for the commodity
questions.explanation: At a price below equilibrium quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, encouraging rationing and black markets.

questions.stem: A minimum wage fixed above the equilibrium wage rate is likely to lead to
options: a fall in the wage rate
an increase in the demand for labour
questions.explanation: A floor above equilibrium raises quantity of labour supplied and reduces quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

questions.stem: An increase in demand for garri with supply unchanged will lead to
options: a rise in both equilibrium price and quantity
a rise in price and a fall in quantity
a fall in price and a rise in quantity
no change in price but a rise in the quantity traded
a fall in both price and quantity
questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand along an upward-sloping supply curve raises both price and quantity.

questions.stem: If supply of yam increases while demand for yam decreases, the equilibrium price will
options: fall, while the effect on quantity is uncertain
rise, while the effect on quantity is uncertain
questions.explanation: Both shifts push price down; supply rising raises quantity while demand falling lowers it, so the net effect on quantity is indeterminate.

questions.stem: The sale of goods at prices above the official controlled price is called
questions.explanation: Trading illegally above a controlled price is black (parallel) marketing.

questions.stem: Rationing is often introduced when a government fixes a maximum price because
options: producers are making too much profit
there is an excess supply of the good
quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at that price
questions.explanation: Rationing distributes limited supplies fairly when shortages arise under maximum price control.

questions.stem: In a Kano tailoring workshop, one worker cuts the fabric, another sews and a third does the embroidery. This arrangement is
questions.explanation: Breaking production into separate tasks, each performed by different workers, is division of labour.

questions.stem: A limitation of division of labour is
questions.explanation: Specialisation pays only when the market is large enough to absorb the larger output.

questions.stem: The output of a cassava farm as more workers are employed is: 1 worker, 10 bags; 2 workers, 24 bags; 3 workers, 36 bags; 4 workers, 44 bags. The marginal product of the third worker is
From the same farm data (4 workers produce 44 bags), the average product at four workers is
questions.explanation: AP = TP/L = 44/4 = 11 bags.

questions.stem: A farmer keeps adding workers to a fixed one-hectare plot. According to the law of variable proportions,
options: total product will fall from the start
questions.explanation: Beyond some point, each extra unit of the variable factor adds less to total output.

questions.stem: On a poultry farm, the extra output from hiring one more attendant exceeds the output per attendant. It follows that
options: average product is at its maximum
questions.explanation: If the extra unit adds more than the average, it pulls the average up.

questions.stem: A large flour mill in Lagos gains a cost advantage that arises from its own expansion. This would be
options: a skilled labour force in the locality
the development of good roads in the area
bulk buying of wheat at a discount
firms supplying spare parts in the area
questions.explanation: Internal economies arise from the firm's own growth; the others are external economies shared by firms in an area or industry.

questions.stem: External economies of scale are enjoyed by a firm as a result of
options: the growth of the industry or concentration of firms in an area
an increase in the firm's own output
the firm's use of better machines
the firm buying raw materials in bulk
questions.explanation: External economies come from outside the firm, such as shared infrastructure and ancillary firms around an industrial area.

questions.stem: Costs which do not change as output changes in the short run are called
questions.explanation: Fixed costs such as rent and insurance remain the same whatever the level of output.

questions.stem: A bakery has total fixed cost of ₦50,000 and total variable cost of ₦150,000 when it produces 1,000 loaves. The average total cost per loaf is
If the total cost of producing 5 units is ₦2,400 and that of producing 6 units is ₦2,700, the marginal cost of the sixth unit is
Average revenue is calculated as
options: change in total revenue divided by change in output
total revenue divided by quantity sold
questions.explanation: AR = TR/Q, which equals price when all units sell at one price.

questions.stem: The economist's concept of cost differs from the accountant's because the economist includes
options: the opportunity cost of resources owned by the firm
the cost of raw materials only
only cash payments to outside suppliers
questions.explanation: Economic cost adds implicit (opportunity) costs, such as the owner's forgone salary, to explicit money costs.

questions.stem: A firm sells 20 units at ₦50 each and 21 units at ₦49 each. The marginal revenue of the 21st unit is
In the short run, the average fixed cost curve
questions.explanation: AFC = TFC/Q; a fixed total is spread over more units, so AFC keeps falling.

questions.stem: The marginal revenue product of labour is
options: the wage paid to the last worker employed
the marginal physical product of labour multiplied by marginal revenue
total revenue divided by the number of workers
the change in total cost from hiring one more worker
questions.explanation: MRP = MPP × MR; it measures the addition to total revenue from employing one more worker.

questions.stem: The marginal cost curve cuts the average cost curve at
options: the point where output is zero
the point where average cost is rising fastest
the point where average fixed cost is lowest
the highest point of the average cost curve
the lowest point of the average cost curve
questions.explanation: When MC is below AC, AC falls; when above, AC rises; so MC crosses AC at its minimum.

questions.stem: A market in which no single seller or buyer can influence the price must have
options: barriers to the entry of new firms
prices set by one dominant firm
many firms selling a homogeneous product
a single seller of the product
heavy competitive advertising by every seller
questions.explanation: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers of an identical product with free entry and exit.

questions.stem: The demand curve facing a single firm under perfect competition is
options: perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price
questions.explanation: The firm is a price taker and can sell any quantity at the ruling price.

questions.stem: A profit-maximising firm in any market structure produces where
options: total cost is at its lowest
price equals average variable cost at its lowest point
total revenue is at its maximum
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where MC = MR (with MC cutting MR from below).

questions.stem: Firms in a perfectly competitive industry earn supernormal profits this year. When the industry reaches long-run equilibrium, each firm will earn
questions.explanation: Free entry competes away abnormal profit, leaving P = minimum AC and only normal profit.

questions.stem: A firm in the short run should shut down if the price falls below
options: average total cost including normal profit
questions.explanation: If price does not cover AVC the firm loses less by closing, losing only its fixed costs.

questions.stem: Product differentiation through brand names and packaging is a major feature of
questions.explanation: Many firms sell close but differentiated substitutes under monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a necessary condition for successful price discrimination?
options: The product is sold in a perfectly competitive market
The markets can be kept separate and have different elasticities of demand
All buyers have the same elasticity of demand
Buyers can easily resell between markets
There are many sellers of the product
questions.explanation: Discrimination works only if markets are separated (no resale) and their demand elasticities differ.

questions.stem: A market situation in which there is only one seller of a product with no close substitute is called
questions.explanation: A monopoly is a sole seller of a product without close substitutes.

questions.stem: A market dominated by a few large firms, such as the mobile telephone networks in Nigeria, is described as
questions.explanation: An industry dominated by a few large interdependent sellers is an oligopoly.

questions.stem: The liability of a sole proprietor for the debts of the business is
options: limited to the value of shares held
questions.explanation: A sole trader is personally liable for all business debts, so liability is unlimited.

questions.stem: A major advantage of a limited liability company over a partnership is that
options: it is easier and cheaper to form
its accounts are kept secret from the public
decisions are taken quickly by one person
it pays no tax on its profits
shareholders' liability is limited to the unpaid amount on their shares
questions.explanation: Limited liability protects members' personal assets beyond their share capital.

questions.stem: A business organisation formed by people with a common interest to promote the economic welfare of its members is
questions.explanation: Co-operatives are owned and controlled by members for their mutual benefit.

questions.stem: When the Federal Government transfers ownership of an electricity company it owns to private investors, the policy is called
questions.explanation: Privatisation transfers ownership from the state to private hands; commercialisation keeps state ownership but requires the enterprise to run profitably.

questions.stem: The policy by which government takes over the ownership of privately owned enterprises is called
questions.explanation: Nationalisation transfers private enterprises to state ownership.

questions.stem: Nigeria's indigenisation policy of the 1970s aimed mainly at
options: encouraging foreigners to buy Nigerian companies
transferring ownership and control of businesses to Nigerians
reducing the number of public enterprises
fixing the prices of imported goods
questions.explanation: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decrees of the 1970s reserved some businesses for Nigerians and required Nigerian equity in others.

questions.stem: A source of long-term finance available to a public limited company but not to a sole proprietor is
options: the sale of shares to the public on the stock exchange
questions.explanation: Only a public company can raise capital by offering shares to the general public.

questions.stem: A common problem of public enterprises in Nigeria which commercialisation seeks to solve is
options: the unlimited liability of their managers
excessive profits paid to private shareholders
inefficiency arising from dependence on government subsidies
lack of government interest in their activities
questions.explanation: Commercialisation makes public enterprises operate on business lines and fund themselves, reducing waste and dependence on subventions.

questions.stem: In the chain of distribution, the middleman who buys goods in bulk from manufacturers and sells in smaller lots to retailers is the
questions.explanation: The wholesaler links producers and retailers by buying in bulk and breaking bulk.

questions.stem: A retailer in Aba renders a service to consumers mainly by
options: selling goods in small quantities near where they live
manufacturing the goods sold in the shop
importing goods in large quantities only
fixing the prices of goods for producers
questions.explanation: Retailers make goods available in convenient quantities and locations for final consumers.

questions.stem: A manufacturer of cosmetics who opens its own shops to sell directly to consumers is said to be
options: eliminating the wholesaler and the retailer
acting as an agent of the wholesaler
questions.explanation: Selling through its own outlets bypasses independent middlemen.

questions.stem: Tomatoes grown in Kaduna often rot before reaching buyers in Port Harcourt. This points to a distribution problem caused mainly by
options: very low demand for tomatoes in the south
poor roads and inadequate storage facilities
the absence of any traders in the market
too many good roads in rural areas
an oversupply of cold rooms in every town
questions.explanation: Bad roads, high transport costs and inadequate storage raise distribution costs and cause wastage.

questions.stem: A government agency whose work helps ensure that goods distributed in Nigeria meet approved quality standards is the
options: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) in Abuja
questions.explanation: SON sets and enforces product standards, protecting consumers in the distribution system.

questions.stem: Co-operative retail societies help their members mainly by
options: buying goods in bulk and selling to members at fair prices
fixing the prices of all goods in the market
questions.explanation: Consumer co-operatives cut out some middlemen and share surpluses among members.

questions.stem: The Malthusian theory of population states that population tends to increase
options: at the same rate as food supply
in geometric progression while food supply increases in arithmetic progression
in arithmetic progression while food supply increases in geometric progression
questions.explanation: Malthus argued population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8…) and food arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4…).

questions.stem: In a country, the population aged under 15 years is 40 million, those aged 65 and above number 5 million and those aged 15 to 64 number 55 million. The dependency ratio is approximately
questions.explanation: Dependency ratio = (40 + 5)/55 × 100 = 81.8%.

questions.stem: A country is said to be over-populated when
options: it has the highest population in its region
its population exceeds what its resources can support at a good standard of living
its birth rate equals its death rate
most of its people live in rural areas
questions.explanation: Over-population is defined relative to resources: per capita output would rise if population were smaller.

questions.stem: A major cause of rural–urban migration in Nigeria is
options: the concentration of jobs and social amenities in cities
the high cost of living in cities
lack of land for farming in urban areas
a high rate of crime in villages
questions.explanation: People move to towns in search of jobs, education, electricity and other amenities.

questions.stem: A population with a high birth rate and a falling death rate will have an age structure in which
options: the working population is the only group
the dependency ratio is very low
the number of old people exceeds the number of young people
a large proportion of the people are young dependants
most people are aged above 65 years
questions.explanation: Such populations have a broad-based age pyramid with many children.

questions.stem: A census provides data that help government mainly to
options: plan the provision of schools, hospitals and other services
fix the prices of goods in markets
determine the exchange rate of the naira
questions.explanation: Population counts and their distribution guide planning and the sharing of resources.

questions.stem: In compiling labour statistics, the National Bureau of Statistics counts as part of the labour force
options: people of working age who are employed or actively seeking work
all the people living in the country
questions.explanation: The labour force includes employed people and the unemployed actively looking for work.

questions.stem: A country has a labour force of 80 million people, of whom 6 million are unemployed. The unemployment rate is
questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = 6/80 × 100 = 7.5%.

questions.stem: A graduate who works as a commercial motorcycle rider because he cannot find a job matching his training is
options: not part of the labour force
questions.explanation: Underemployment means working below one's skills or for fewer hours than desired.

questions.stem: Unemployment that results from a general fall in aggregate demand during a recession is called
questions.explanation: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment rises during the downswing of the trade cycle.

questions.stem: Investment in education, health and training of workers is referred to as
questions.explanation: Spending that raises the skills and productivity of people builds human capital.

questions.stem: A trade union may succeed in raising wages without large job losses if
options: the demand for its members' labour is very elastic
the demand for the labour it represents is inelastic

the very low population of the country

questions.stem:
The demand schedule for loaves of bread at a bakery in Oshogbo is shown below.
Price per loaf (₦): 800, 1,000, 1,200, 1,400, 1,600
Quantity demanded (loaves per day): 500, 450, 360, 250, 120
(a) Calculate the total revenue at each price. [5 marks]
(b) Using the original price and quantity in each case, calculate the price elasticity of demand when price rises (i) from ₦1,000 to ₦1,200; (ii) from ₦1,200 to ₦1,400. [6 marks]
(c) Comment on the type of elasticity in (b)(i) and (b)(ii). [3 marks]
(d) Explain two ways in which knowledge of price elasticity of demand is useful to the government. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) TR = ₦400,000; ₦450,000; ₦432,000; ₦350,000; ₦192,000 (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(i) %ΔQ = 90/450 x 100 = 20% (1); %ΔP = 200/1,000 x 100 = 20% (1); PED = 20/20 = 1 (1)
3 marks: (b)(ii) %ΔQ = 110/360 x 100 = 30.56% (1); %ΔP = 200/1,200 x 100 = 16.67% (1); PED = 30.56/16.67 = 1.83 (1)
3 marks: (c) (i) unitary elasticity, TR almost unchanged/elasticity equals one (1.5); (ii) elastic, coefficient greater than one so TR falls when price rises (1.5)
6 marks: (d) Any two well explained, 3 marks each: choosing goods to tax (inelastic goods raise more revenue); predicting incidence of indirect taxes; deciding on devaluation/exchange-rate policy; fixing prices of public utilities; deciding which goods to subsidise or control
questions.explanation: (a) TR = P x Q gives ₦400,000, ₦450,000, ₦432,000, ₦350,000 and ₦192,000. (b)(i) Quantity falls by 90 from 450 (20%) as price rises by 20%, so PED = 1. (ii) Quantity falls by 110 from 360 (30.56%) as price rises by 16.67%, so PED = 1.83. (c) The first is unitary elastic demand; the second is elastic, so a price rise there reduces total revenue (₦432,000 to ₦350,000). (d) Government uses elasticity to select goods for taxation, since taxing goods with inelastic demand yields more revenue; to predict how much of a tax consumers will bear; to judge whether devaluation will improve the trade balance; and to set tariffs for utilities.

questions.stem:
The table below shows the total utility Ngozi derives from eating meat pies in one afternoon.
Number of meat pies: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total utility (utils): 20, 36, 48, 56, 60, 60
(a) Calculate the marginal utility of each meat pie. [6 marks]
(b) Calculate the average utility at each level of consumption. [6 marks]
(c) At what number of meat pies is marginal utility zero? What happens to total utility at that point? [3 marks]
(d) State the law of diminishing marginal utility. [2 marks]
(e) State the condition for consumer equilibrium when a consumer buys two goods, X and Y. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) MU = 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0 (1 mark each)
6 marks: (b) AU = 20, 18, 16, 14, 12, 10 (1 mark each)
3 marks: (c) The 6th meat pie (1); total utility is at its maximum/stops rising at 60 utils (2)
2 marks: (d) As more units of a commodity are consumed successively, the additional satisfaction from each extra unit eventually declines, other things being equal (2)
3 marks: (e) MUx/Px = MUy/Py (2) with the whole income spent (1)
questions.explanation: (a) MU is the change in TU: 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 and 0 utils. (b) AU = TU/Q: 20, 18, 16, 14, 12 and 10 utils. (c) MU is zero at the sixth pie, where total utility reaches its maximum of 60 utils. (d) The law states that, other things being equal, as a consumer takes more units of a good in succession, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls. (e) The consumer is in equilibrium when the marginal utility per naira spent is equal for both goods, MUx/Px = MUy/Py, and all income is spent.

questions.stem:
The demand and supply functions for a brand of yoghurt are:
Qd = 240 − 4P
Qs = −60 + 6P
where P is price in naira and Q is quantity in cartons.
(a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity. [6 marks]
(b) The government fixes a maximum price of ₦25. Calculate the quantity demanded, the quantity supplied and the resulting shortage. [6 marks]
(c) Explain two likely consequences of the maximum price in (b). [4 marks]
(d) Explain what is meant by a minimum price and give one example of its use in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Set 240 − 4P = −60 + 6P (2); 300 = 10P so P = ₦30 (2); Q = 240 − 120 = 120 cartons (2)
6 marks: (b) Qd = 240 − 100 = 140 cartons (2); Qs = −60 + 150 = 90 cartons (2); shortage = 50 cartons (2)
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: black market/parallel market; queues; rationing; hoarding; sellers reducing quality; reduced supply in long run
4 marks: (d) A legal price floor set above equilibrium below which a good/service may not be sold (2); example: national minimum wage or guaranteed minimum prices for farm produce (2)
questions.explanation: (a) At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 240 − 4P = −60 + 6P, so 10P = 300, P = ₦30 and Q = 120 cartons. (b) At ₦25, Qd = 140 and Qs = 90, giving a shortage of 50 cartons. (c) The shortage encourages black marketing at prices above ₦25, long queues, rationing, hoarding and possibly a fall in quality. (d) A minimum price is a floor fixed above equilibrium; in Nigeria the national minimum wage is a floor on wages, and guaranteed minimum prices have been used to protect farmers.

questions.stem:
A small sachet-water factory in Abeokuta has the following total costs (₦'000) at different levels of output (in thousands of sachets).
Output: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total cost: 100, 160, 200, 230, 280, 350, 450
(a) What is the total fixed cost? Give a reason. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total variable cost at each level of output from 1 to 6. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the average total cost at each level of output from 1 to 6, to two decimal places where necessary. [3 marks]
(d) Calculate the marginal cost of each unit of output from 1 to 6. [3 marks]
(e) At what output is average total cost lowest? Explain the relationship between marginal cost and average total cost shown by your figures. [4 marks]
(f) If each thousand sachets sells for ₦70,000, calculate the profit or loss at an output of 5 (thousand sachets). [2 marks]
(g) Distinguish between fixed cost and variable cost. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) TFC = ₦100,000 (1) because cost at zero output is fixed cost (1)
3 marks: (b) TVC = 60, 100, 130, 180, 250, 350 (₦'000) (3 marks: deduct 1 per error)
3 marks: (c) ATC = 160, 100, 76.67, 70, 70, 75 (₦'000) (3 marks: deduct 1 per error)
3 marks: (d) MC = 60, 40, 30, 50, 70, 100 (₦'000) (3 marks: deduct 1 per error)
4 marks: (e) Lowest ATC is ₦70,000 at outputs 4 and 5 (2); when MC is below ATC, ATC falls; when MC is above, ATC rises; MC (70) equals ATC (70) at the minimum (2)
2 marks: (f) TR = 5 x 70 = 350 (1); TC = 350 so profit = 0, the firm breaks even (normal profit) (1)
3 marks: (g) Fixed costs do not vary with output and are incurred even at zero output, e.g. rent (1.5); variable costs change with output, e.g. raw materials, fuel (1.5)
questions.explanation: (a) TFC is ₦100,000, the cost incurred when output is zero. (b) TVC = TC − TFC: 60, 100, 130, 180, 250, 350 thousand naira. (c) ATC = TC/Q: 160, 100, 76.67, 70, 70, 75. (d) MC = change in TC: 60, 40, 30, 50, 70, 100. (e) ATC is lowest (₦70,000) at outputs of 4 and 5; while MC is below ATC (outputs 2 to 4) ATC falls, and once MC exceeds ATC (output 6) ATC rises, with MC equal to ATC at the minimum. (f) TR = 5 x ₦70,000 = ₦350,000 = TC, so the firm breaks even. (g) Fixed costs such as rent stay the same at all outputs in the short run; variable costs such as raw materials vary directly with output.

questions.stem:
The table shows the total output of tubers of yam on a farm in Benue State when workers are added to a fixed piece of land.

(b) Calculate the average product at each level of employment, to one decimal place where necessary. [6 marks]
(c) At what number of workers does diminishing marginal returns set in? [2 marks]
(d) State the law of variable proportions. [3 marks]
(e) Explain the relationship between marginal product and average product shown in your answers. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) MP = 8, 12, 16, 12, 7, 2 (1 mark each)
6 marks: (b) AP = 8, 10, 12, 12, 11, 9.5 (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) After the third worker / with the fourth worker, when MP falls from 16 to 12 (2)
3 marks: (d) As more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, MP and AP first rise but eventually decline, other things being equal (3)
3 marks: (e) When MP > AP, AP rises (1); when MP < AP, AP falls (1); MP = AP when AP is at its maximum (here 12 at 3 to 4 workers) (1)
questions.explanation: (a) MP is the change in TP: 8, 12, 16, 12, 7 and 2 hundred tubers. (b) AP = TP/L: 8, 10, 12, 12, 11 and 9.5. (c) Diminishing marginal returns set in with the fourth worker, whose MP (12) is below the third worker's (16). (d) The law states that when more and more of a variable factor is applied to a fixed factor, marginal and average product rise at first but eventually fall. (e) AP rises while MP exceeds it, stays at its peak where MP equals it, and falls once MP is below it.

2 marks: (a)(ii) GNP = 102 + (−4) = ₦98 trillion (2)
2 marks: (a)(iii) NNP = 98 − 6 = ₦92 trillion (2)
3 marks: (a)(iv) NI = NNP − indirect taxes + subsidies = 92 − 9 + 2 (2) = ₦85 trillion (1)
2 marks: (b) Expenditure method (2)
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: measuring standard of living (per capita income); comparing living standards between countries/over time; economic planning; measuring growth; showing the structure of the economy/sector contributions; guiding fiscal and monetary policy; basis for contributions to international organisations
questions.explanation: (a) GDP = 60 + 20 + 25 + 15 − 18 = ₦102 trillion; GNP = 102 − 4 = ₦98 trillion; NNP = 98 − 6 = ₦92 trillion; NI at factor cost = 92 − 9 + 2 = ₦85 trillion. (b) Adding final spending is the expenditure method. (c) National income figures are used to measure living standards through per capita income, compare countries and periods, measure the rate of growth, show the contribution of each sector, guide planning and fiscal and monetary policy, and assess contributions to bodies such as the IMF.

questions.stem:
(a) The marks obtained by ten SS3 students in an Economics test were:
45, 52, 48, 70, 52, 55, 47, 52, 58, 51
Calculate the (i) mean; (ii) median; (iii) mode. [9 marks]
(b) A family in Owerri spends its monthly income as follows: food ₦72,000; rent ₦36,000; transport ₦24,000; school fees ₦30,000; others ₦18,000. Calculate the angle of each sector if the data are shown on a pie chart. [6 marks]
(c) State one advantage and one disadvantage of the mean as a measure of central tendency. [2 marks]
(d) Name three types of graphs or charts used to present economic data. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) Sum = 530 (2); mean = 530/10 = 53 (2)
3 marks: (a)(ii) Arranged: 45, 47, 48, 51, 52, 52, 52, 55, 58, 70 (1); median = (52 + 52)/2 = 52 (2)
2 marks: (a)(iii) Mode = 52 (occurs three times) (2)
6 marks: (b) Total = ₦180,000 (1); food 144°, rent 72°, transport 48°, school fees 60°, others 36° (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Advantage: uses all values/easy to calculate (1); disadvantage: affected by extreme values such as 70 (1)
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: bar chart; pie chart; line graph; histogram; pictogram; component bar chart
questions.explanation: (a) The marks total 530, so the mean is 53; arranged in order the two middle marks are 52 and 52, so the median is 52; 52 occurs three times, so the mode is 52. (b) Total spending is ₦180,000; each angle is amount/180,000 x 360°: food 144°, rent 72°, transport 48°, school fees 60° and others 36°. (c) The mean uses every value but is pulled up by extremes such as 70. (d) Bar charts, pie charts, line graphs, histograms and pictograms are common.

questions.stem:
The following items (₦ billion) relate to the external transactions of an imaginary country in one year.
Visible exports: 8,400
Visible imports: 6,900
Invisible exports (services): 1,100
Invisible imports (services): 2,600
Net current transfers (including diaspora remittances): +2,300
Net capital and financial flows: −900
(a) Calculate (i) the balance of trade; (ii) the balance on invisibles; (iii) the current account balance; (iv) the overall balance. [8 marks]
(b) What will happen to the country's external reserves as a result of your answer in (a)(iv)? [2 marks]
(c) Explain five measures a country may adopt to correct a persistent balance of payments deficit. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) 8,400 − 6,900 = +₦1,500 billion (surplus) (2)
2 marks: (a)(ii) 1,100 − 2,600 = −₦1,500 billion (deficit) (2)
2 marks: (a)(iii) 1,500 − 1,500 + 2,300 = +₦2,300 billion (2)
2 marks: (a)(iv) 2,300 − 900 = +₦1,400 billion (surplus) (2)
2 marks: (b) External reserves will increase by ₦1,400 billion (the surplus is added to reserves) (2)
10 marks: (c) Any five, 2 marks each: devaluation/depreciation of the currency; tariffs and import restrictions/quotas; export promotion and incentives; exchange control; deflationary monetary policy (higher interest rates); deflationary fiscal policy; import substitution; borrowing from IMF while adjusting; encouraging foreign investment and tourism
questions.explanation: (a) Balance of trade = 8,400 − 6,900 = ₦1,500 billion surplus; balance on invisibles = 1,100 − 2,600 = −₦1,500 billion; current account = 1,500 − 1,500 + 2,300 = ₦2,300 billion surplus; overall balance = 2,300 − 900 = ₦1,400 billion surplus. (b) The overall surplus adds ₦1,400 billion to official reserves. (c) A deficit can be corrected by devaluation, tariffs and quotas, export promotion, exchange control, tight monetary and fiscal policy that reduce spending on imports, import substitution, and by attracting foreign investment, with IMF borrowing as temporary finance.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem:
(a) What is a mixed economy? [3 marks]
(b) State four features of a capitalist economy. [8 marks]
(c) Explain three disadvantages of a socialist (command) economy. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) An economic system in which both the private sector and the government own resources and take economic decisions, with prices and planning both used (3)
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: private ownership of means of production; profit motive; price mechanism allocates resources; consumer sovereignty; freedom of enterprise and choice; competition; limited government intervention
9 marks: (c) Any three, 3 marks each: lack of incentive to work hard/innovate; restricted consumer choice; bureaucracy and inefficiency in planning; shortages and queues; poor quality goods; loss of individual freedom; misallocation of resources without price signals
questions.explanation: (a) A mixed economy combines private enterprise with state ownership and control, so both the market and government planning answer the basic questions; Nigeria is an example. (b) Capitalism features private ownership of resources, the profit motive, allocation through the price mechanism, consumer sovereignty, freedom of enterprise and competition. (c) Socialism suffers from weak incentives because profits and property belong to the state, limited consumer choice, inefficient bureaucratic planning that causes shortages and poor-quality goods, and restriction of individual economic freedom.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the Malthusian theory of population. [6 marks]
(b) Give three criticisms of the theory. [6 marks]
(c) Explain four problems encountered in conducting a population census in Nigeria. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8…) (2); food supply grows arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4…) (2); population tends to outstrip food, checked by positive checks (famine, disease, war) or preventive checks (late marriage, moral restraint) (2)
6 marks: (b) Any three, 2 marks each: ignored technological advances in agriculture; ignored birth control/family planning; food production in many countries has grown faster than population; emigration/trade can relieve pressure; population is also a productive resource
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: illiteracy and ignorance; religious and cultural beliefs; political manipulation/inflation of figures; poor transport to remote areas; inadequate funding and personnel; insecurity; inaccurate maps/demarcation; lack of reliable birth and death registration
questions.explanation: (a) Malthus argued that population, unchecked, grows in geometric progression while food grows in arithmetic progression, so population tends to outrun food until positive checks (famine, disease, war) or preventive checks (moral restraint, late marriage) restore balance. (b) He underestimated agricultural technology, ignored modern birth control, was contradicted by food output in many countries, and overlooked trade and emigration. (c) Nigerian censuses face illiteracy, cultural and religious resistance, political inflation of figures because census data affect revenue sharing and representation, difficult terrain, insecurity, poor funding and inaccurate enumeration area maps.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between unemployment and underemployment. [4 marks]
(b) Explain four types of unemployment. [8 marks]
(c) Suggest four measures the government of Nigeria can take to reduce youth unemployment. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Unemployment: people willing and able to work at current wages cannot find jobs (2); underemployment: people work below their skills/capacity or for fewer hours than they want (2)
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: frictional; structural; cyclical/demand-deficient; seasonal; technological; disguised; voluntary (each with a brief explanation)
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: skills acquisition and vocational training; support for small businesses/credit to entrepreneurs; investment in agriculture and agro-processing; improving power and infrastructure to attract industry; reviewing the school curriculum to match labour market needs; labour-intensive public works; attracting foreign investment
questions.explanation: (a) An unemployed person cannot find work at all despite being willing and able; an underemployed person is working but below their capacity or for fewer hours than desired, such as a graduate doing casual labour. (b) Frictional unemployment occurs while people move between jobs; structural unemployment results from changes in the structure of the economy; cyclical unemployment arises from falling aggregate demand; seasonal unemployment follows seasons, as in farming; technological unemployment follows automation. (c) Government can expand vocational training, give credit and support to small businesses, invest in agriculture and agro-processing, fix power and infrastructure, align the curriculum with employers' needs and run labour-intensive public works.

questions.stem:
(a) State four characteristics of a monopoly. [8 marks]
(b) Explain how a monopolist determines its profit-maximising output and price. [6 marks]
(c) Explain three conditions necessary for a monopolist to practise price discrimination successfully. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any four, 2 marks each: single seller; no close substitutes; barriers to entry; price maker; downward-sloping demand/AR curve; MR below AR; can earn supernormal profit in the long run
6 marks: (b) Produces where MC = MR (2) with MC cutting MR from below (1); price is read from the AR/demand curve at that output (2), giving price above MC/supernormal profit where AR > AC (1)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: markets can be separated (no resale); different price elasticities in the markets; monopoly power/no competitors; cost of separating markets lower than gains; consumer ignorance or inertia
questions.explanation: (a) A monopolist is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry; it is a price maker facing the downward-sloping market demand curve, so MR lies below AR, and it can keep supernormal profit in the long run. (b) It maximises profit by producing where MC = MR, then charges the highest price consumers will pay for that output, read from the demand (AR) curve; if AR exceeds AC it earns supernormal profit. (c) Price discrimination needs separable markets so goods cannot be resold, different elasticities of demand (charge more where demand is inelastic), and enough monopoly power, with separation costs below the extra revenue.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between privatisation and commercialisation of public enterprises. [4 marks]
(b) Explain four reasons why the Federal Government of Nigeria privatised some public enterprises. [8 marks]
(c) Explain four disadvantages of privatisation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Privatisation: sale of all or part of government shares/ownership of an enterprise to private investors (2); commercialisation: government keeps ownership but the enterprise must run on commercial lines and fund itself, charging economic prices (2)
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: inefficiency and poor services of public enterprises; reduce burden of subsidies on government budget; raise revenue for government; attract private/foreign investment and technology; widen share ownership; reduce corruption and political interference; improve competition
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: higher prices/tariffs for consumers; job losses through restructuring; concentration of wealth in few hands; assets sold below true value; private monopoly may replace public monopoly; foreign domination of key sectors; neglect of unprofitable but essential services
questions.explanation: (a) Privatisation transfers ownership of a public enterprise to private investors, while commercialisation leaves ownership with government but requires the enterprise to operate profitably without subventions. (b) Government privatised because many enterprises were inefficient and loss-making, subsidies strained the budget, sales raised revenue, private capital and technology were needed, and political interference and corruption hampered performance. (c) Privatisation can bring higher prices, retrenchment, sale of assets below value, concentration of wealth, private monopolies and neglect of services that are not profitable.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four functions of money. [8 marks]
(b) State the quantity theory of money using Fisher's equation of exchange, explaining each symbol. [6 marks]
(c) In an economy M = ₦800 billion, V = 5 and T = 2,000 billion transactions. (i) Calculate the price level P. (ii) If M rises to ₦1,200 billion with V and T unchanged, calculate the new price level. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any four, 2 marks each: medium of exchange; unit of account/measure of value; store of value; standard of deferred payment; means of transferring value
6 marks: (b) MV = PT (2); M = quantity of money, V = velocity of circulation, P = general price level, T = volume of transactions (1 each)
3 marks: (c)(i) P = MV/T = (800 x 5)/2,000 (2) = 2 (1)
3 marks: (c)(ii) P = (1,200 x 5)/2,000 (2) = 3 (1)
questions.explanation: (a) Money serves as a medium of exchange, removing the double coincidence of wants; a unit of account for measuring value; a store of value; and a standard of deferred payment for loans and credit. (b) Fisher's equation MV = PT, where M is money supply, V velocity, P price level and T transactions; with V and T constant, P varies directly with M. (c) P = (800 x 5)/2,000 = 2; with M = 1,200, P = (1,200 x 5)/2,000 = 3, a 50% rise matching the 50% rise in M.

questions.stem:
(a) What is inflation? [3 marks]
(b) Explain three causes of inflation in Nigeria. [9 marks]
(c) Explain four effects of inflation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) A persistent/sustained rise in the general price level over a period, which reduces the purchasing power of money (3)
9 marks: (b) Any three, 3 marks each: excess money supply/deficit financing (demand-pull); rising cost of production such as fuel, transport and wages (cost-push); depreciation of the naira raising import prices (imported inflation); insecurity reducing food supply; hoarding and speculation; poor infrastructure raising costs
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: fall in real income of fixed income earners; debtors gain, creditors lose; discourages saving; balance of payments problems (exports dearer); redistribution of income; uncertainty discouraging investment; industrial unrest/wage demands; producers may gain from rising prices
questions.explanation: (a) Inflation is a persistent rise in the general level of prices, so each naira buys less. (b) In Nigeria inflation has come from rapid growth in money supply and deficit financing, cost-push pressures from fuel, transport and energy prices, naira depreciation raising import prices, and insecurity that disrupts food production. (c) Its effects include falling real incomes for pensioners and salary earners, a gain for debtors at creditors' expense, reduced saving, uncompetitive exports, uncertainty that discourages investment, and agitation for higher wages.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria. [8 marks]
(b) A deposit money bank receives a new deposit of ₦400,000. The cash reserve ratio is 12.5% and banks lend out all excess reserves. Calculate (i) the credit multiplier; (ii) the total deposits created in the banking system; (iii) the total new loans created. [6 marks]
(c) State three factors that limit the ability of commercial banks to create credit. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any four, 2 marks each: issue of currency; banker to government; banker to banks/lender of last resort; controlling money supply/monetary policy; managing external reserves and exchange rate; supervising and regulating banks; managing public debt with the DMO
2 marks: (b)(i) Multiplier = 1/0.125 = 8 (2)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Total deposits = 400,000 x 8 = ₦3,200,000 (2)
2 marks: (b)(iii) New loans = 3,200,000 − 400,000 = ₦2,800,000 (2)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: cash reserve ratio/liquidity requirements set by CBN; availability of creditworthy borrowers/collateral; public's preference for holding cash (cash leakages); CBN monetary policy rate/credit controls; size of deposits
questions.explanation: (a) The CBN issues the naira, acts as banker to government and to banks, serves as lender of last resort, conducts monetary policy, manages external reserves and the exchange rate, and supervises banks. (b) The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8; total deposits = ₦400,000 x 8 = ₦3,200,000; new loans = ₦3,200,000 − ₦400,000 = ₦2,800,000. (c) Credit creation is limited by reserve and liquidity requirements, cash withdrawals by the public, the supply of creditworthy borrowers with collateral, and CBN credit and interest rate policy.

questions.stem:
A state government applies the following hypothetical personal income tax schedule on annual taxable income:
First ₦300,000: 0%
Next ₦500,000: 10%
Next ₦1,200,000: 15%
Above ₦2,000,000: 20%
(a) Calculate the tax payable and the average rate of tax for persons with taxable incomes of (i) ₦700,000; (ii) ₦1,500,000; (iii) ₦3,000,000. Give average rates to two decimal places. [9 marks]
(b) Is this tax system progressive, proportional or regressive? Give a reason from your answers. [3 marks]
(c) Explain four canons of taxation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 0 + 10% x 400,000 = ₦40,000 (2); average rate = 5.71% (1)
3 marks: (a)(ii) 0 + 50,000 + 15% x 700,000 = ₦155,000 (2); average rate = 10.33% (1)
3 marks: (a)(iii) 0 + 50,000 + 180,000 + 20% x 1,000,000 = ₦430,000 (2); average rate = 14.33% (1)
3 marks: (b) Progressive (1) because the average rate rises from 5.71% to 10.33% to 14.33% as income rises (2)
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: equity (according to ability to pay); certainty (amount, time and manner clear); convenience (collected at a convenient time and way); economy (cost of collection low); flexibility; productivity; simplicity
questions.explanation: (a) On ₦700,000 the first ₦300,000 is free and ₦400,000 is taxed at 10%, giving ₦40,000 (5.71%). On ₦1,500,000: ₦50,000 on the second band plus 15% of ₦700,000 = ₦105,000, total ₦155,000 (10.33%). On ₦3,000,000: ₦50,000 + ₦180,000 + 20% of ₦1,000,000 = ₦430,000 (14.33%). (b) The system is progressive because the proportion of income paid in tax rises with income. (c) Adam Smith's canons are equity (tax according to ability to pay), certainty (the taxpayer knows what, when and how to pay), convenience (collection at a suitable time and in a suitable manner) and economy (collection costs small relative to yield); flexibility and productivity are modern additions.

questions.stem:
With one unit of resources, Nigeria can produce either 12 tubers of yam or 4 metres of cloth, while Togo can produce either 6 tubers of yam or 3 metres of cloth.
(a) Which country has an absolute advantage in producing both goods? [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the opportunity cost of (i) 1 metre of cloth and (ii) 1 tuber of yam in each country. [8 marks]
(c) Using your answers, state which good each country should specialise in, and give a reason. [4 marks]
(d) Within what range must the terms of trade (tubers of yam per metre of cloth) lie for both countries to gain? [2 marks]
(e) State two limitations of the theory of comparative cost advantage. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Nigeria (12 > 6 yam; 4 > 3 cloth) (2)
4 marks: (b)(i) Cloth: Nigeria 12/4 = 3 tubers of yam (2); Togo 6/3 = 2 tubers of yam (2)
4 marks: (b)(ii) Yam: Nigeria 4/12 = 1/3 metre of cloth (2); Togo 3/6 = 1/2 metre of cloth (2)
4 marks: (c) Nigeria should specialise in yam, its opportunity cost of yam (1/3 m) is lower (2); Togo should specialise in cloth, its opportunity cost of cloth (2 tubers) is lower (2)
2 marks: (d) Between 2 and 3 tubers of yam per metre of cloth (2)
4 marks: (e) Any two, 2 marks each: assumes no transport costs; assumes free trade without tariffs; assumes constant costs/full employment; ignores immobility of factors; considers only two countries and two goods; ignores strategic/security goods
questions.explanation: (a) Nigeria produces more of both goods per unit of resources, so it has absolute advantage in both. (b) In Nigeria 1 m of cloth costs 3 tubers of yam and 1 tuber costs 1/3 m of cloth; in Togo 1 m of cloth costs 2 tubers and 1 tuber costs 1/2 m of cloth. (c) Nigeria has the lower opportunity cost in yam and Togo in cloth, so Nigeria should specialise in yam and Togo in cloth. (d) Both gain if 1 m of cloth exchanges for more than 2 but fewer than 3 tubers. (e) The theory ignores transport costs and trade barriers, assumes constant costs and mobile factors within countries, and considers only two goods and two countries.

questions.stem:
(a) What is economic integration? [3 marks]
(b) State five objectives of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). [10 marks]
(c) Explain three problems that have hindered the achievement of ECOWAS objectives. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) An arrangement whereby countries in a region agree to remove trade barriers among themselves and co-ordinate economic policies to promote trade and development (3)
10 marks: (b) Any five, 2 marks each: promote trade among members by removing tariffs; free movement of persons, goods and services; common external tariff; co-operation in agriculture, industry, transport and energy; harmonise economic and monetary policies/single currency; raise living standards; promote peace and regional stability; develop infrastructure linking members
7 marks: (c) Any three explained (first two 2 marks, third 3 marks): political instability and coups/withdrawal of some members; different currencies and monetary systems; poor transport and communication links; similar primary exports limiting trade; loyalty to former colonial powers; non-implementation of protocols/border harassment; smuggling and insecurity
questions.explanation: (a) Economic integration is the coming together of countries to remove trade barriers and co-ordinate economic policies. (b) ECOWAS aims to promote intra-regional trade by abolishing tariffs, ensure free movement of people, goods and services, adopt a common external tariff, co-operate in agriculture, industry, energy and transport, harmonise monetary policies towards a single currency, and raise living standards in peace and stability. (c) Progress has been slowed by political instability and the 2025 withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, multiple currencies, poor transport links, members producing similar primary goods, ties to former colonial powers and failure to implement protocols at borders.

questions.stem:
(a) Name three natural resources found in West Africa and a country in which each is mainly produced. [6 marks]
(b) Explain four positive effects of petroleum on the Nigerian economy. [8 marks]
(c) Explain three negative effects of petroleum on the Nigerian economy. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Any three pairs, 2 marks each: petroleum, Nigeria; gold, Ghana; diamonds, Sierra Leone; bauxite, Guinea; iron ore, Liberia; timber, Côte d'Ivoire; phosphate, Togo; uranium, Niger
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: main source of government revenue; major source of foreign exchange; provides employment; raw materials for petrochemical industries; attracts foreign investment; infrastructure development; source of energy/fuel; contribution to GDP
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: neglect of agriculture; mono-product economy vulnerable to oil price shocks (Dutch disease); environmental pollution, oil spills and gas flaring; conflicts and insecurity in the Niger Delta; corruption and rent-seeking; rural-urban migration
questions.explanation: (a) West African resources include petroleum in Nigeria, gold in Ghana, diamonds in Sierra Leone, bauxite in Guinea, iron ore in Liberia and timber in Côte d'Ivoire. (b) Petroleum provides most of Nigeria's export earnings and a large share of government revenue, creates jobs, attracts foreign investment, supplies raw materials and energy, and has financed infrastructure. (c) It has also led to neglect of agriculture and dependence on one volatile export, pollution from spills and gas flaring, conflict in the Niger Delta, and corruption.
